title: The one who prostrates
hook: Ali Zayn al-Abidin, who survived Karbala, leaves prayers gathered in al-Sahifa al-Sajjadiyya

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zaynab's voice: a captive who shielded her nephew in Kufa and spoke before Yazid in Damascus. Your line was: zaynab spoke. What true thing did you say, and to whom? Day eight hundred ninety-three.

The boy Zaynab shielded in Kufa lived. He was Ali, Husayn's son, too sick on the day of Karbala to fight, and he grew into a man who went back to Medina. He did not raise an army. He did not make speeches against the palace in Damascus. What people remembered about him was quieter and stranger: how often, and how long, he lay with his forehead on the ground. They gave him names for it. Zayn al-Abidin, the ornament of the worshippers. And al-Sajjad. Today: the one who prostrates.
screen: `THE BOY WHO LIVED.` → `NO ARMY, NO SPEECHES.` → `HIS FOREHEAD ON THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: Al-Sajjad is tied to sujud, the prostration of prayer, when the forehead touches the ground. Tradition explains the name as one who does it again and again: the one of prostrations. For Shia Muslims, Ali Zayn al-Abidin is the fourth Imam. Sunni scholars honored him too; the hadith scholar al-Zuhri, who knew him in Medina, is reported to have praised him warmly. What he left behind is a book of prayers. It is called al-Sahifa al-Sajjadiyya, the pages of al-Sajjad, and in Shia tradition it is treasured as words of an Imam addressed to God. Open it and the range is wide. There are prayers for the morning and the evening, for the new moon, for the coming of Ramadan. There is a prayer for his parents, asking that he might be gentle with them and lower his voice before them. There is a prayer for his children. There is a prayer for his neighbors and friends, asking for the grace to visit the sick among them, to give without being asked, to cover their faults. There is even a prayer for the soldiers guarding the frontiers. A man who had lost his father and brothers at Karbala prays for ordinary people's kitchens and doorsteps. Tradition adds a story told about him by Sunni and Shia writers alike. Families in Medina, the story goes, found sacks of bread at their doors by night and never knew from whom. When he died, the bread stopped, and those who washed his body found marks on his back from carrying it. Whatever grief he carried, he turned it into prostration, and into bread.
screen: `SUJUD: THE FOREHEAD ON THE GROUND.` · `THE FOURTH IMAM.` · `PRAYERS FOR PARENTS AND NEIGHBORS.` · `BREAD AT THE DOOR BY NIGHT.` · then, large: `THE ONE OF PROSTRATIONS.`

segments.voice: The practice: read one of his prayers. Translations of the Sahifa can be found online; later today, find one and choose the prayer for parents, or for neighbors. For now, settle, and breathe. Take what his neighbor prayer asks for and hold it: visit the sick, give before being asked, cover a fault instead of exposing it. Breathe in, and bring one neighbor to mind. Breathe out, and ask which of those three you could do for them this week. If you pray, you can bow your head, or put your forehead to the ground. The bell holds the time.
The one who prostrates. Ali Zayn al-Abidin, al-Sajjad, who survived Karbala and left the prayers gathered in al-Sahifa al-Sajjadiyya. Today's word.
Your line: the one of prostrations. Today, do one kindness for a neighbor without letting them know it came from you. Day eight hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Shia Muslims read the supplications of al-Sahifa al-Sajjadiyya, the prayers of the fourth Imam, privately and in gatherings, often on particular days and occasions the prayers themselves name.

original.note: Arabic: the one who prostrates often, from sujud, prostration.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'the one who prostrates' just means a pious man.
what it means: al-Sajjad, a title for Ali Zayn al-Abidin, who survived Karbala and is remembered for his prostrations and his prayers.
what a scholar hears: the fourth Imam of the Shia, praised by Sunni hadith scholars such as al-Zuhri, whose supplications fill al-Sahifa al-Sajjadiyya.
